Most corrections move “sporadic” townships that were not significant in the final quarter into “No pattern detected”. The table also catches three townships in Shan that sfdep called intensifying hot spots for explosions and remote violence. They were cold spots in almost every quarter and slowly warming, which the lecture calls diminishing cold spots.

Step 4. Where hot spots are emerging

The brief asks for EHSA maps that show only townships with a significant Mann-Kendall trend (p < 0.05). That rule has a blind spot. A township that is hot in nearly every quarter has no trend, so it can never pass the filter. To keep that in view, the trend map sits beside a second map that counts how many of the 19 quarters each township was a significant hot spot.

  • The Plot
  • The Code
tot_map <- ehsa_map %>% filter(variable == "All armed conflict") %>%
  mutate(hot_band = cut(hot_q, c(-1, 0, 4, 9, 14, 19),
                        labels = c("Never", "1 to 4", "5 to 9", "10 to 14", "15 to 19")))
m1 <- tm_shape(tot_map) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "shown", fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = ehsa_cols, levels.drop = TRUE),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "EHSA pattern, p < 0.05", position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom"),
                                      frame = FALSE),
              col = "white", lwd = 0.15) +
  state_borders + state_names +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE) +
  tm_title("Trend, where hot spots are emerging or fading", size = 1.1, fontface = "bold")
m2 <- tm_shape(tot_map) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "hot_band", fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = c("#F7F2EA", "#FDD0A2", "#FD8D3C", "#D94801", "#7F2704")),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Quarters as a\nsignificant hot spot", position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom"),
                                      frame = FALSE),
              col = "white", lwd = 0.15) +
  state_borders +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE) +
  tm_title("Persistence, how often each township was hot", size = 1.1, fontface = "bold")
tmap_arrange(m1, m2, ncol = 2)

The core stayed hot, and the conflict spread around it. 151 of 330 townships have a significant trend. The right map shows why the Sagaing core is mostly blank on the left. Its High-High townships were significant hot spots in 10 to 18 of the 19 quarters, a steady heat with no clear rise or fall. The growing hot spots form a ring around that core. 5 consecutive hot spots, which turned hot late and stayed hot, sit in the hills of Bago (East) and on the road from Mandalay to northern Shan. 30 oscillating hot spots, cold earlier and hot by the end, run through Tanintharyi, Mon, central Rakhine, Bago (East) and the south of the Dry Zone. On the cold side, Yangon has 39 of its 45 townships in a cold pattern. Six townships on the northern Shan border were the hottest anywhere in late 2023 and turned cold after it. The readings below take each pattern in turn.

What each pattern looks like over time

Each panel shows the EHSA Gi* series of every township in one pattern, in grey, with their median in colour. The shaded bands mark significant hot (above 1.96) and cold (below −1.96) values.

  • The Plot
  • The Code
series <- ehsa_all$total$gi %>%
  inner_join(sig_tot %>% select(TS_PCODE, pattern), by = "TS_PCODE") %>%
  add_count(pattern, time, name = "n_ts") %>%
  mutate(panel = paste0(pattern, " (", n_ts, ")"),
         panel = fct_reorder(panel, match(pattern, ehsa_levels)))
med <- series %>% group_by(panel, pattern, time) %>% summarise(gi = median(gi_star), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(series, aes(time, gi_star)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = 1.96, ymax = Inf, fill = "#FBE7DA", alpha = 0.6) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = -Inf, ymax = -1.96, fill = "#DDE9F4", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(aes(group = TS_PCODE), colour = "grey75", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(data = med, aes(y = gi, colour = pattern), linewidth = 1.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = ehsa_cols, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 9, 17), labels = c("2021", "2023", "2025")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-3, 10)) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 4) +
  labs(title = "Hot patterns climbed after 2022, while Yangon's cold patterns slid steadily",
       x = NULL, y = "Gi*") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"), strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11.5),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

Reading each pattern

Consecutive hot spots, 5 townships. These are the clearest new hot spots. Shwegyin, Kyaukkyi, Mogoke, Kyaukme, Nawnghkio were not hot in 2021 but became hot and stayed hot to the end, with their median Gi* rising from about zero to between 3 and 7. They mark two new fronts. One is the hills of Bago (East) next to Kayin, around Kyaukkyi and Shwegyin. The other is the road from Mandalay to northern Shan, through Mogoke, Nawnghkio and Kyaukme, where fighting moved in the second phase of Operation 1027 in 2024. Both lead from the edge of the country towards its centre, so they are where the conflict is still advancing.

Oscillating hot spots, 30 townships. This is the largest hot pattern. Each township was a significant cold spot at least once, usually in 2021, and is hot in the final quarter. They fall in four groups. 9 cover most of Tanintharyi, from Dawei to Kawthoung. 4 are in central Rakhine, around Kyaukpyu and Ramree, which were cold in 2021 and turned hot in 2024 as fighting moved south through the state. 4 are in Mon and 4 in Bago (East). The rest are in the Dry Zone, mostly in its south around Myingyan, Taungtha, Chauk and Salin, plus Singu on the road to northern Shan. These are the places where conflict arrived during the study period.

Sporadic hot spots, 6 townships. These are hot in the final quarter and were hot on and off before, but never cold. 4 of them are in Kayin, including Kawkareik, Myawaddy and Hpa-An on the Thai border. They were strongest in 2025, so the south-east border is warming again after a quieter 2023.

Oscillating cold spots, 25 townships. These were hot at least once and are cold now. 6 are on the Chinese border in northern Shan, including Laukkaing, Hseni and Kunlong. They were the hottest places in Myanmar in late 2023, the spike in Figure 11, when Operation 1027 began, and turned cold after the ceasefire brokered by China in early 2024. The other 19 are in Yangon and around Mandalay city, slightly warm during the urban resistance of 2021 and cold since.

Intensifying, consecutive and sporadic cold spots, 29 townships. The 9 intensifying cold spots are all in Yangon, including downtown Pazundaung, Botahtaung and Lanmadaw, and they grow colder each year. Thanlyin is a consecutive cold spot. The sporadic cold spots are mostly in Yangon and the delta. Together they show the conflict draining out of Myanmar’s largest city.

No pattern detected, 56 townships. These have a significant trend but fit none of the patterns, usually because they were not significant in the final quarter. They split into two groups. 29 are falling, led by Chin, Kachin, Mandalay and the north-west of Sagaing, where conflict peaked in 2021 or 2022 and faded. 27 are rising, 13 of them in Bago (West), including Okpho from Figure 9. They are warming from cold but are not yet hot spots, so they are the townships to watch next.

Step 5. How each type of violence is moving

The same analysis is repeated for each conflict variable in the cube.

  • The Plot
  • The Code
tm_shape(ehsa_map %>% filter(variable %in% ehsa_vars[c("battles", "remote", "civilians")]) %>%
           mutate(variable = factor(fct_drop(variable), labels = c("Battles", "Explosions", "Attacks on civilians")))) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "shown", fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = ehsa_cols, levels.drop = TRUE),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "EHSA pattern,\np < 0.05", position = tm_pos_out("right", "center"),
                                      frame = FALSE),
              col = "white", lwd = 0.1) +
  tm_facets(by = "variable", ncol = 3) +
  tm_shape(mmr_st) + tm_borders(col = "grey25", lwd = 0.5) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE, panel.label.size = 1.1, panel.label.bg.color = "white", panel.label.frame = FALSE) +
  tm_title("Battles moved to the coasts, explosions to Bago and the south,\nand attacks on civilians to Bago (West)",
           size = 1.1, fontface = "bold")

Battles, 101 townships with a significant trend. Ground fighting moved to the coast and the far south. 22 townships turned from cold to hot, led by Tanintharyi (6) and central Rakhine (6), where the Arakan Army pushed south in 2024. The clearest cooling is in northern Shan, where 8 townships, from Lashio to Laukkaing, were hot during Operation 1027 and cold after the 2024 ceasefire. Battles also have the weakest trends. Only about half survive the checks in Step 7, possibly because ground fighting jumps from place to place rather than building steadily.

Explosions and remote violence, 131 townships. Explosions spread into the hills between the Dry Zone and Kayin, and down the south. 19 townships turned from cold to hot, led by Tanintharyi (7) and Bago (East) (6). Hpakant in Kachin is a new hot spot, and Shwegyin in Bago (East) and Hpapun in Kayin are consecutive ones. Yangon and the delta grew colder, as the bombings of 2021 and 2022 faded. Three townships in southern and eastern Shan are diminishing cold spots, cold throughout but slowly warming.

Violence against civilians, 142 townships. This type moved most clearly. 7 of its 14 oscillating hot spots are in Bago (West), including Letpadan, Thayarwady, Minhla and Okpho, an area of little fighting that became a hot spot for attacks on civilians. The rest are in the south of the Dry Zone. Meanwhile the far north-west, Kale, Kalewa and Ye-U in Sagaing and Falam and Tedim in Chin, and Kayah turned from hot to cold. Attacks on civilians are moving south towards the lowlands, into areas that see little fighting.

Step 6. The military’s air strikes

Figure 3 showed that the military’s air strikes rose about 23-fold. They are the one part of the war that can reach any township, so they get a map of their own.

  • The Plot
  • The Code
tm_shape(ehsa_map %>% filter(variable == "Military air strikes")) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "shown", fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = ehsa_cols, levels.drop = TRUE),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "EHSA pattern, p < 0.05", position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom"),
                                      frame = FALSE),
              col = "white", lwd = 0.15) +
  state_borders + state_names +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE) +
  tm_title("Air strikes turned hot across the Dry Zone\nand on most new fronts", size = 1.1, fontface = "bold")

The air campaign grew most in the ground war’s core and on most of its new fronts. 178 townships have a significant trend in military air strikes. 29 are oscillating hot spots, cold in 2021 when strikes were rare and hot by the end. They cover the Sagaing core (6), Magway (7), the road to northern Shan, the hills of Bago (East) and Dawei in Tanintharyi, many of the same places as the new ground fronts in Figure 10. Central Rakhine is the exception, with only Myebon among them. This changes how the Sagaing core reads. Ground events there drifted down, but air strikes on it kept growing. Hpakant in Kachin is a consecutive hot spot, and nearby Myitkyina, Mohnyin and Mogaung are sporadic ones. Most cold patterns, in Yangon, the delta and Shan (East), simply mean these places were rarely bombed while strikes grew elsewhere. For civilians this means the threat from the air grew most where ground fighting was also growing.

Step 7. How much to trust the trends

The Lesson 5 notes warn that the Mann-Kendall test assumes no serial correlation, that is, each quarter’s value should not depend on the last. Conflict breaks this rule, because a busy quarter is usually followed by another. The table measures how strong this is, and re-tests every trend two ways. The Hamed and Rao modified Mann-Kendall test, mmkh() from modifiedmk, widens the test to allow for serial correlation. The false discovery rate correction allows for running 330 tests at once.

serial correlation, corrected trend test and FDR
trend_check <- map_dfr(names(ehsa_vars), function(v) {
  g <- ehsa_all[[v]]$gi %>% arrange(TS_PCODE, time) %>% group_by(TS_PCODE) %>%
    summarise(ac1 = acf(gi_star, lag.max = 1, plot = FALSE)$acf[2],
              p_hr = mmkh(gi_star)[["new P-value"]])
  e <- ehsa_all[[v]]$ehsa
  both <- e %>% select(TS_PCODE = location, p_value) %>% left_join(g, by = "TS_PCODE")
  tibble(variable = ehsa_vars[[v]],
         median_lag1 = round(median(g$ac1, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
         significant = sum(both$p_value < 0.05),
         after_fdr = sum(p.adjust(both$p_value, "fdr") < 0.05),
         modified_mk = sum(both$p_value < 0.05 & both$p_hr < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE))
})
trend_check %>% kable(col.names = c("Variable", "Median lag-1 autocorrelation", "Significant at p < 0.05",
                                    "Still significant after FDR", "Still significant under modified Mann-Kendall"))
Variable Median lag-1 autocorrelation Significant at p < 0.05 Still significant after FDR Still significant under modified Mann-Kendall
All armed conflict 0.65 151 121 114
Battles 0.65 101 46 62
Explosions and remote violence 0.58 131 106 119
Violence against civilians 0.61 142 101 118
Military air strikes 0.60 178 170 175

Most trends survive, but battle trends are fragile. The median lag-1 autocorrelation is around 0.6 for every variable, so the plain Mann-Kendall p-values are too optimistic, as the lecture warns. Still, most significant trends survive both checks. For all armed conflict, 121 of 151 remain after FDR and 114 under the modified test. Explosions and military air strikes hold up even better. Battles are the exception, with only 46 of 101 surviving FDR, so the battle map in Figure 12 should be read as a guide, not a firm result. The maps keep the brief’s p < 0.05 rule, and these numbers say how much weight each one can bear.

Bonus. The Kind of Violence, Multivariate Local Geary’s c

NoteShort answer

Neighbouring townships mostly face the same kind of violence, but not everywhere. Multivariate local Geary’s c finds a group of 29 townships, 16 in Yangon and 7 around Mandalay city, where battles are rare but bombs and attacks on civilians are common, and where neighbours share that mix. Local Moran’s I treats every one of them as quiet or not significant. The pattern is growing. Around Mandalay, townships that saw all three types in 2021 and 2022 had shifted to this mix by 2023 to 2025, and in Yangon it moved from downtown to the outskirts. Only 2 townships have a mix clearly unlike their neighbours’.

Why this question, and why this method

The first objective asks where violence clusters or “behaves unusually compared to surrounding townships”. Task 2 answered that for the amount of violence, one type at a time. But the same total can hide very different wars. A township of ground battles needs front-line medical care and safe routes out. A township of bombings and killings in a city needs protection and monitoring. Task 2 cannot see this difference, because it never looks at the three types together.

The Lesson 5 notes list local Geary’s c under “Other forms of LISA” but it was not covered in class. Its multivariate form (Anselin, 2019) compares a township’s whole profile of several variables with its neighbours’ profiles. A small value means the township and its neighbours share the same mix, a cluster in the kind of violence. A large value means the township’s mix is unlike its neighbours’, an outlier in kind. Both answer the first objective, extended from how much violence to what kind.

Question
Do neighbouring townships face the same mix of battles, explosions and attacks on civilians, and where does the mix cluster or stand out?
Method
Multivariate local Geary’s c, local_c_perm() from sfdep, on the three conflict variables.
Null model
Conditional permutation of whole township profiles, 999 shuffles. A positive result means neighbours are more alike than chance, a negative one less alike.
Assumptions
The three types are put on one scale first. Counts are log-transformed, log(1 + count), to calm the skew, then standardised. Each type weighs the same.
Settings
8 nearest neighbours, row-standardised weights, p < 0.05, checked with FDR and with 6 and 10 neighbours.

Step 1. Computing the statistic

multivariate local Geary's c
z_log <- function(x) as.numeric(scale(log1p(x)))
geary_in <- wm_knn %>%
  mutate(z_battles = z_log(battles), z_remote = z_log(remote), z_civilians = z_log(civilians))

profile_of <- function(p, cl, zb, zr, zc) case_when(
  p >= 0.05 ~ "Not significant",
  cl == "Negative" ~ "Mix unlike its neighbours",
  zb > 0 & zr > 0 & zc > 0 ~ "All three high",
  zb < 0 & zr < 0 & zc < 0 ~ "All three low",
  zb < 0 ~ "Few battles, more bombs or attacks on civilians",
  TRUE ~ "Mostly battles")
profile_levels <- c("All three high", "Mostly battles", "Few battles, more bombs or attacks on civilians",
                    "All three low", "Mix unlike its neighbours", "Not significant")

set.seed(1234)
geary <- geary_in %>%
  mutate(local_c = local_c_perm(list(z_battles, z_remote, z_civilians), nb, wt, nsim = 999), .before = 1) %>%
  unnest(local_c) %>%
  mutate(profile = factor(profile_of(p_ci_sim, cluster, z_battles, z_remote, z_civilians), levels = profile_levels))

Step 2. Naming the groups from the data

local_c_perm() only says whether a township is like its neighbours or unlike them. To say what the shared mix is, each significant township is grouped by which of its three standardised values are above the national average. The table checks that the names match the data. It gives each group’s average standardised value and its share of each type, against the national shares.

what each group's mix really is
nat <- colSums(st_drop_geometry(mmr_conflict)[, c("battles", "remote", "civilians")]) / sum(mmr_conflict$total)
f1 <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", ifelse(abs(x) < 0.05, 0, x))   # avoids printing -0.0
shares <- function(b, r, c) paste(round(100 * b), round(100 * r), round(100 * c), sep = " / ")
geary %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(profile) %>%
  summarise(townships = n(),
            z_mix = paste(f1(mean(z_battles)), f1(mean(z_remote)), f1(mean(z_civilians)), sep = " / "),
            share = shares(sum(battles) / sum(total), sum(remote) / sum(total), sum(civilians) / sum(total))) %>%
  add_row(profile = "Myanmar as a whole", share = shares(nat[["battles"]], nat[["remote"]], nat[["civilians"]])) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Group", "Townships", "Average z, battles / explosions / civilians",
                      "Share of events %, battles / explosions / civilians"),
        align = c("l", "r", "c", "c"))
Group Townships Average z, battles / explosions / civilians Share of events %, battles / explosions / civilians
All three high 72 1.0 / 0.9 / 0.9 41 / 41 / 18
Mostly battles 8 0.5 / 0.2 / 0.0 46 / 39 / 15
Few battles, more bombs or attacks on civilians 29 -0.6 / 0.2 / 0.4 10 / 54 / 36
All three low 77 -1.2 / -1.1 / -1.0 18 / 46 / 36
Mix unlike its neighbours 2 0.4 / 0.0 / -1.2 62 / 31 / 7
Not significant 142 0.2 / 0.0 / 0.0 41 / 42 / 16
Myanmar as a whole 39 / 42 / 18

The battle shares confirm the names. In the group called “few battles, more bombs or attacks on civilians”, battles are only 10 percent of events against 39 percent nationally. Its share of attacks on civilians, 36 percent, is high, but the all-low group has a similar share. What sets this group apart is the combination. Its townships have few battles, yet above-average numbers of bombs or attacks on civilians, while the all-low townships have little of anything.

  • The Code
geary_cols <- c("All three high" = col_high, "Mostly battles" = col_hl,
                "Few battles, more bombs or attacks on civilians" = "#CC79A7", "All three low" = col_low,
                "Mix unlike its neighbours" = "#000000", "Not significant" = col_ns)

tm_shape(geary) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "profile",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = geary_cols, levels.drop = TRUE),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Shared mix, p < 0.05", position = tm_pos_out("right", "center"),
                                      frame = FALSE),
              col = "white", lwd = 0.2) +
  state_borders +
  # Yangon and Mandalay are left unnamed here so the labels do not cover the townships this map is about
  tm_shape(filter(st_lab, !ST %in% c("Yangon", "Mandalay"))) +
  tm_text("ST", size = 0.55, col = "grey5", bgcol = "white", bgcol_alpha = 0.65) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE) +
  tm_title("Yangon and Mandalay city share a mix\nof bombs and attacks on civilians",
           size = 1.1, fontface = "bold")

Two big groups are expected, and one is new. 188 townships share their mix with their neighbours more than chance allows. 72 have all three types high, led by Sagaing (22), Magway and Mandalay, with Rakhine and Tanintharyi. 77 have all three low, in the delta and eastern and southern Shan. The third group is the new finding. 29 townships, 16 in Yangon and 7 in Mandalay, mostly in and around the two cities, have few battles but above-average bombs or attacks on civilians. Insein in Yangon, for example, had 5 battles but 93 explosions and 56 attacks on civilians. This fits urban bombings and targeted killings rather than front-line war. Only 2 townships have a mix unlike their neighbours’. Kalewa in Sagaing recorded no attacks on civilians at all, unlike the townships around it, and Laukkaing on the Chinese border had a battle-heavy mix its neighbours did not share.

Step 3. What this adds to Task 2

Geary groups against the local Moran's I classes
geary %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(lisa = factor(as.character(lisa$quadrant), levels = c("High-High", "Low-Low", "Low-High", "Not significant"))) %>%
  filter(profile != "Not significant") %>%
  mutate(profile = fct_drop(profile)) %>%
  count(profile, lisa, .drop = FALSE) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = lisa, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Geary group", "LISA High-High", "LISA Low-Low", "LISA Low-High", "LISA not significant"))
Geary group LISA High-High LISA Low-Low LISA Low-High LISA not significant
All three high 33 0 0 39
Mostly battles 0 0 0 8
Few battles, more bombs or attacks on civilians 0 6 0 23
All three low 0 62 0 15

The urban group is invisible to a count-based map. Of the 29 bombs-and-civilians townships, 23 are not significant in local Moran’s I and 6 are Low-Low. Looking at totals, they are quiet places. Looking at the mix, they share a distinct kind of violence that calls for protection of civilians in cities rather than front-line aid. Geary’s c also widens the hot core. It finds 72 all-high townships where local Moran’s I found 34 High-High, because it asks whether neighbours share the mix, not whether totals are extreme.

Step 4. Is the mix changing?

The second objective asks in what pattern violence is evolving. The same test is run on two periods, January 2021 to December 2022 and January 2023 to September 2025, to see whether the groups held still.

Geary's c for the early and late periods
period_geary <- function(qs, label) {
  counts <- cube_counts %>% filter(quarter %in% qs) %>% group_by(TS_PCODE) %>%
    summarise(across(c(battles, remote, civilians), sum))
  d <- wm_knn %>% select(TS_PCODE, TS, ST, nb, wt) %>% left_join(counts, by = "TS_PCODE")
  zb <- z_log(d$battles); zr <- z_log(d$remote); zc <- z_log(d$civilians)
  set.seed(1234)
  g <- local_c_perm(list(zb, zr, zc), d$nb, d$wt, nsim = 999)
  d %>% mutate(period = label,
               profile = factor(profile_of(g$p_ci_sim, g$cluster, zb, zr, zc), levels = profile_levels))
}
geary_time <- bind_rows(period_geary(quarters[1:8], "2021 to 2022"),
                        period_geary(quarters[9:19], "2023 to 2025"))

geary_time %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(profile == "Few battles, more bombs or attacks on civilians") %>%
  count(period, ST) %>% pivot_wider(names_from = period, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("State or region", "2021 to 2022", "2023 to 2025"))

Around Mandalay the mix is spreading, and in Yangon it moved outward. In Mandalay the group grew from 3 to 8 townships, and in Magway from 2 to 5. 8 townships had all three types high in 2021 and 2022 and moved into this group by 2023 to 2025. 6 are in Mandalay region, Chanayethazan, Mahaaungmyay, Chanmyathazi, Pyigyitagon, Kyaukse, Wundwin, and 2 on the edge of Yangon, Mingaladon and Hlaingtharya. Battles fell away there, but bombings and attacks on civilians did not. Yangon kept 14 townships in this group in both periods, but only 7 were the same. The group moved from the downtown townships, such as Botahtaung and Lanmadaw, to the industrial outskirts, such as Hlaingtharya and Mingaladon. This fits the outward spread found in Task 3.

Step 5. How much to trust the groups

FDR and different numbers of neighbours
urban_ids <- geary$TS_PCODE[geary$profile == "Few battles, more bombs or attacks on civilians"]
k_check <- map_dfr(c(6, 8, 10), function(k) {
  nb_k <- st_knn(centres, k = k); wt_k <- st_weights(nb_k, style = "W")
  set.seed(1234)
  g <- local_c_perm(list(geary$z_battles, geary$z_remote, geary$z_civilians), nb_k, wt_k, nsim = 999)
  prof <- profile_of(g$p_ci_sim, g$cluster, geary$z_battles, geary$z_remote, geary$z_civilians)
  tibble(neighbours = k, significant = sum(g$p_ci_sim < 0.05),
         urban_kept = sum(prof[geary$TS_PCODE %in% urban_ids] == "Few battles, more bombs or attacks on civilians"))
})
k_check %>% kable(col.names = c("Neighbours", "Significant townships", "Bombs-and-civilians townships kept (of 29)"))
Neighbours Significant townships Bombs-and-civilians townships kept (of 29)
6 173 27
8 188 29
10 202 27 
tibble(group = c("All significant townships", "Bombs-and-civilians group"),
       significant = c(sum(geary$p_ci_sim < 0.05), length(urban_ids)),
       after_fdr = c(sum(p.adjust(geary$p_ci_sim, "fdr") < 0.05),
                     sum(p.adjust(geary$p_ci_sim, "fdr")[geary$TS_PCODE %in% urban_ids] < 0.05))) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Group", "Significant at p < 0.05", "Still significant after FDR"))
Group Significant at p < 0.05 Still significant after FDR
All significant townships 188 165
Bombs-and-civilians group 29 25

The urban group is stable. Almost all of its townships stay in it with 6 or 10 neighbours, and most survive the FDR correction.

Assumptions and limitations of the bonus

Assumption or limit Effect How it was handled
The three types are logged and standardised, and weigh the same A different weighting, for example by fatalities, could change the groups Stated. The group shares in Step 2 show the names follow the raw counts
Groups use the sign of each standardised value A township just above the national average counts as high Group averages in Step 2 are well away from zero
Small townships in Yangon have low counts The urban group rests on tens of events per township Checked with FDR and with 6 and 10 neighbours
Geary’s c is a similarity measure It cannot say why neighbours share a mix Read together with Task 2 and Task 3, not alone

Integrated Findings and Discussion

Each method answers a different question, so the strongest findings are the ones they agree on.

Finding Task 1, maps Task 2, clusters Task 3, trends Bonus, mix How sure
The Dry Zone is the core of the war 43 percent of events, 6 of the 10 busiest townships 28 of 34 High-High, 31 of 40 hot spots Hot in 10 to 18 of 19 quarters, with no steady trend 44 of 72 all-high townships Very sure, every method agrees
Conflict spread outward from the core Rakhine and Bago grew year after year Second clusters differ by type 5 consecutive and 30 oscillating hot spots ring the core Rakhine and Tanintharyi join the all-high group Sure for all conflict, weaker for battles alone
Yangon emptied of fighting but not of violence Events fell sharply after 2022 26 Low-Low, 26 cold spots 39 of 45 townships in a cold pattern 16 townships share a bombs-and-civilians mix Sure
Northern Shan flared and cooled Peak in late 2023 Not a cluster over the whole period 6 border townships turned from hot to cold Sure, the spike is very large
Air strikes follow the ground war Military air strikes rose about 23-fold Explosions cluster in the core and on the Bago and Kayin edge 29 oscillating air hot spots, in the core and on the new fronts Sure, these trends survive every check

Three lessons come from reading the methods together.

  1. Where conflict is, where it clusters and where it is growing are three different maps. Kawkareik is the second busiest township but sits in no cluster. The Sagaing core is the hottest neighbourhood but is blank on the trend map, because its heat never changed. A planner using only one of these maps would miss something important.
  2. The war widened rather than moved. The core stayed hot while new hot spots opened around it, from the hills of Bago (East) and the road to northern Shan to central Rakhine and the far south. Townships in Bago (West) are warming but are not yet hot spots, which makes them the likeliest next ones.
  3. When fighting leaves, the violence changes kind. Around Mandalay, battles moved away after 2022 but bombs and attacks on civilians stayed. Yangon has had this mix all along, though it moved from downtown to the outskirts. Count-based maps call these places quiet. The mix says they are not.

Geovisualisation and Geocommunication

Four design choices shape every figure.

Design choice Why
Every title states the finding, and a short reading below each figure leads with the insight The reader knows what to look for, within the word limits
Warm colours for hot and high, blue for cold and low, pale beige for not significant The eye goes straight to significant results, and no map depends on telling red from green
Counts use one orange scale with fixed breaks, and types and years are small multiples Darker always means more, and panels can be compared directly
The EHSA trend map sits beside a map of how often each township was hot The brief’s p < 0.05 trend filter hides steady hot spots, and the second map shows them

Peace-keeping Implications

The brief hopes the results can help peace-building and prevent further conflict. The table links each finding to an action that peace-keepers, ceasefire monitors or aid agencies could consider, and to what should be checked first. ACLED records reported events, not need or harm, and the analysis shows where and when, not why or who is responsible. Each row is therefore a starting point for planning, not a conclusion.

Finding Possible action Check first
The Dry Zone core has been a hot spot in most quarters for almost five years Plan long-term health, protection and displacement support there, rather than short emergency surges Displacement and access data from UN agencies and local partners
New hot spots are opening around the core, in Bago (East), on the Mandalay to northern Shan road, in central Rakhine and the far south Use these as an early-warning list. Pre-position supplies and safe-route plans before conflict peaks Whether local partners see the same spread, and which roads are still open
Bago (West) is warming but not yet hot, and several of its townships turned into hot spots for attacks on civilians Watch it closely for protection risks to civilians Local reports, since events there may be under-reported
The military’s air strikes keep returning to the core and the new fronts Support early warning, shelters and trauma care in these townships Casualty records, because strike counts do not show harm
Yangon and Mandalay city share a mix of bombs and attacks on civilians Treat them as settings for civilian protection and monitoring, not front-line aid Under-reporting in cities under tight control
Northern Shan turned from the hottest area to a cold spot after the early 2024 ceasefire Monitor the ceasefire townships for relapse, and study what made the ceasefire hold Whether the ceasefire still holds, and what it meant for the people living there

Limitations

Limitation Effect on the results How it was handled
ACLED records reported events Places with less media or internet access, such as Rakhine during blackouts, may look calmer than they are Low-High outliers are flagged as possibly under-reported
Counts, not rates A busy town may look high because more happens there No reliable population for 2021 to 2025 was available. Stated wherever it matters
Events, not harm An air strike and a small clash count the same Air strikes are given their own cube
Location precision 43 percent of events are placed at a nearby town Township counts are coarse enough, and the region-level events were checked
Township boundaries ACLED splits some townships, such as Dagon Myothit, that the boundary file keeps whole Events are joined by location, so none are lost, but the splits are not shown
Neighbour reach Remote islands such as Cocokyun have neighbours hundreds of kilometres away Queen contiguity was tested as a check
The trend filter Steady hot spots have no trend and never pass p < 0.05 Figure 10 shows persistence beside the trend map
Serial correlation Plain Mann-Kendall p-values are too optimistic Modified Mann-Kendall and FDR checks in Task 3
Gi* is relative to each quarter A falling Gi* means a smaller share of the conflict, not less conflict Stated where trends are read
sfdep’s EHSA rules Two rules differ from the lecture definitions Corrected and listed in Task 3

Conclusion

Q1. Armed conflict was heaviest in the central Dry Zone, which holds 43 percent of all events, and along the borders. It peaked in late 2023, and the military’s air strikes grew about 23-fold. Q2. Local Moran’s I and Gi* find one large hot cluster in the Dry Zone, a smaller one around Dawei, and cold clusters in Yangon, the delta and eastern Shan. The few outliers are quieter townships beside hot areas, plus Pathein and Thaketa as busy places in quiet areas. Q3. The core stayed hot, while new hot spots opened around it and Yangon and northern Shan cooled. Each type of violence spread in its own direction, and attacks on civilians moved towards the lowlands. Q4. Neighbours mostly share the same mix of violence, but Yangon and Mandalay city share a different one, of bombs and attacks on civilians, which spread as the fighting moved on.

The main lesson is that the war has not shifted from one place to another. It has widened from a core that never cooled, and where the fighting leaves, a different kind of violence often stays.

Future work

  • Rates. Divide counts by township population once reliable estimates for 2021 to 2025 exist, so that busy towns are compared fairly.
  • Harm. Weight events by fatalities, or build a cube of civilian deaths, to map harm rather than activity.
  • A monthly cube for 2023 and 2024. Operation 1027 and the Rakhine offensive moved within months, which a quarterly cube smooths out.
  • Displacement. Join township displacement figures to test whether people flee from emerging hot spots.
